title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (5 of 7)
hook: a baby monkey clings to its mother, a kitten is carried in its mother's mouth, and Ramanuja's followers asked which one you are
carry: two, and the space between is love
tomorrow: Dvaita and beyond (6 of 7): Madhva and the five differences

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dvaita and beyond: Kanakadasa, the shepherd poet singing outside the temple wall at Udupi, and a Krishna who, the story says, turned to face him. Your line: two, and the space between is love. Did you turn toward someone at the edge? Today, back to Ramanuja's people. Day two hundred ninety-two.
screen: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Watch a mother monkey leap from branch to branch. Her baby rides along, holding on to her belly with its own small hands. Now watch a mother cat move her kitten. She picks it up by the scruff of its neck, and the kitten just hangs there, loose, carried. Two babies, two mothers, two ways of getting across. In South India, Ramanuja's later followers argued over these two animals. Because the question underneath them is a big one. When God saves a soul, how much does the soul hold on?
screen: `A BABY MONKEY CLINGS.` → `A KITTEN IS CARRIED.` → `HOW MUCH DOES THE SOUL HOLD ON?`

segments.voice: You met Ramanuja a few days ago, on the temple tower, with the world as God's body. Today, the heart of how his followers practice. They call it prapatti: surrender, taking refuge. Not giving up. Turning to God the way a child turns to a parent, and letting yourself be held. Sri Vaishnavas say Ramanuja himself, at the temple of Srirangam, offered a prose prayer of surrender before Vishnu and Lakshmi, and they still recite it. And they treasure a verse near the end of the Gita, which they call the final verse. In it Krishna says, roughly: let go of every other support, take refuge in me alone, I will free you from every wrong, do not grieve. Later came the question from the hook. One lineage, later called the northern school, taught with the baby monkey: grace carries you, and you also hold on, with your own small effort. The other, the southern school, taught with the kitten: grace does everything, and even your holding on is a gift. Both lineages trace themselves to Ramanuja, and both are alive today. This path doesn't settle it. But notice what both pictures share. In each one there's a mother and a child. Two. Surrender only makes sense if there's someone to surrender to. Advaita, which you met before Madhva and Ramanuja, would say that in the end there's only one. Ramanuja's people say the soul is held, forever, and never stops being the one who is held. That's devotion needing difference. You can't be carried by yourself.
screen: `PRAPATTI: TAKING REFUGE.` · `TAKE REFUGE IN ME ALONE. DO NOT GRIEVE.` · `THE MONKEY HOLDS ON. THE KITTEN IS CARRIED.` · `BOTH TRACE THEMSELVES TO RAMANUJA.` · then, large: `YOU CAN'T BE CARRIED BY YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Sit, and feel the chair or the floor under you. Notice that you aren't holding yourself up right now. Something else is doing that. Let your shoulders drop a little, and let the weight go down. Breathe in, and notice any small effort you're still making, a tight jaw, a held breath. Breathe out, and let one of those go. You don't have to decide whether you're the monkey or the kitten. Just notice what it feels like to be held. If you pray, you can name one worry and leave it with God for these few minutes. The bell holds the time.
Dvaita and beyond, part five. Prapatti, taking refuge, the way of Ramanuja's followers. Clinging like a monkey or carried like a kitten, there is always a mother and a child. Two.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. Today, let someone help you with one thing, and don't take it back halfway. Day two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Many Sri Vaishnavas formally take refuge through a rite called samashrayana, given by a teacher, and recite the dvaya mantra and Gita 18.66 daily; the northern (Vadakalai) and southern (Tenkalai) lineages are often told apart by the shape of the namam, the mark worn on the forehead.

fork.setup: two lineages of Ramanuja's followers disagree: is the soul a baby monkey that clings, or a kitten that's carried? what did the tradition do?
options: keep the monkey and drop the kitten.

keep the kitten and drop the monkey.

original.note: Sanskrit: surrender, taking refuge; from pra + pad, to go forward toward, to approach for shelter.

trapdoor: what you thought: surrender means giving up, or doing nothing.
what it means: prapatti is a real soul taking refuge in a real God, the relationship devotion needs.

what a scholar hears: prapatti or sharanagati; the markata-nyaya (monkey) and marjara-nyaya (cat) analogies, associated with the Vadakalai (Vedanta Desika) and Tenkalai (Pillai Lokacharya) lineages; Gita 18.66 as the charama shloka.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.66 (the charama shloka: take refuge in me alone; do not grieve)
Sharanagati Gadya, traditionally attributed to Ramanuja (the prayer of surrender at Srirangam)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced time spans ('a few generations after', 'for a very long time').

REWRITTEN IN REVIEW: the first draft of this day repeated day 289 almost exactly (the Thirukoshtiyur tower story, the world as God's body, the same carry action). It now teaches prapatti and the later monkey-and-kitten debate instead, so the Ramanuja material is not told twice.

Gita 18.66 is paraphrased ('let go of every other support, take refuge in me alone, I will free you from every wrong, do not grieve'), not quoted. 'Let go of every other support' renders sarva-dharman parityajya, whose meaning is itself debated; confirm the paraphrase.

The Gadya Traya, including the Sharanagati Gadya, is traditionally attributed to Ramanuja and tradition places it at Srirangam on Panguni Uttiram; some scholars question the attribution. The script says 'Sri Vaishnavas say', which keeps it as tradition. Confirm.

The monkey and kitten analogies are associated with the Vadakalai (Vedanta Desika) and Tenkalai (Pillai Lokacharya) lineages respectively. This is a simplification of a long and sometimes sharp debate; the script presents both evenly and does not settle it. Confirm both lineages would accept the one-line summaries ('grace carries you, and you also hold on' / 'grace does everything, and even your holding on is a gift').
howItsDone: samashrayana, the dvaya mantra, and the namam shapes as a sign of lineage; confirm wording.
